note: The registered prediction from isa_floorplans.json, TESTED 27 Aug 2026 across the four floorplans. It FAILED -- and the metric it was built on survived, which is the more useful of the two outcomes and the one this sweep existed to distinguish.
design: 12 points: 4 floorplans x 3 demanded margins. Everything except GEOMETRY held fixed -- same density (0.60 W/mm^2), same margins, same 500 um pitch, same 200 um burial, same uniform activity. scripts/isa_benefit.sh.

PREDICTION_1_FALSIFIED.predicted: a compact core has a NARROWER plateau and a LARGER span
PREDICTION_1_FALSIFIED.measured: plateau 17 -> 59 -> 54 -> 71 and span 30.5 -> 21.1 -> 18.5 -> 16.0 K as the core shrinks. Both are the OPPOSITE of the prediction: compact dies are WIDER-plateaued and MORE thermally uniform.
PREDICTION_1_FALSIFIED.why_I_was_wrong: The reasoning assumed constant die POWER -- less SRAM per watt to buffer the heat. The sweep holds constant density, so a smaller die dissipates LESS TOTAL POWER: unaided peaks fall 63.1 -> 51.9 -> 46.7 -> 42.9 C. A cooler die is a flatter die. The confound was built into the experiment by holding the wrong quantity fixed, and it is mine, not the model's.

PREDICTION_2_NOT_SUPPORTED.predicted: a wide-vector core stands further clear of its runner-up
PREDICTION_2_NOT_SUPPORTED.measured: gap 2.00 (x86, AVX-512) then 0.54 (arm_n2), 0.07 (arm_v1), 0.00 (riscv_p670). x86 does have much the largest gap, but the ordering does NOT follow vector width -- arm_v1 carries the widest non-x86 vector and has essentially none.
PREDICTION_2_NOT_SUPPORTED.what_it_exposes: Scaling the whole core uniformly PRESERVES the unit mix, so the variants inherit a highly degenerate peak: three of four have a gap under 0.6 K. That is a limitation of area re-weighting as a method, not a finding about ARM or RISC-V, and it should be fixed before any vector-width claim is made from these floorplans.

PREDICTION_3_FALSIFIED_and_this_is_the_i.predicted: compact and wide-vector cores are BETTER MR targets -- lower cost per margin
PREDICTION_3_FALSIFIED_and_this_is_the_i.measured: cost at 3 K: x86 0.491 W, arm_n2 0.850, arm_v1 0.921, riscv_p670 1.349. The x86 baseline is the CHEAPEST to cool and the most compact die is the most expensive -- 2.7x. The same ordering holds at 5 K and 8 K.
PREDICTION_3_FALSIFIED_and_this_is_the_i.BUT_THE_METRIC_WAS_RIGHT: rho(relative_plateau, cost) = +1.000 at every one of the three margins. The metric ordered the cost perfectly. What failed was my architectural reasoning about which way the plateau would go -- not the relationship between plateau and cost.

THE_RESULT_THAT_MATTERS: The metric TRANSFERS ACROSS FLOORPLANS. relative_plateau_25pct predicted cost at rho +0.84 across eleven workloads on one die (metric_regression_gen0.json) and at rho +1.00 across four floorplans at one workload. That is the question the workload regression could not answer -- whether a predictor validated on eleven workloads was merely describing that floorplan -- and the answer is no. A metric that survives its designer's prediction being wrong is better evidence than one that agrees with it.
what_this_does_NOT_say: It is NOT a finding that ARM or RISC-V cores are poor MR targets. The variants re-weight AREA with the Skylake-class power trace redistributed over it, at constant density -- so what was actually measured is that SMALLER DIES AT CONSTANT DENSITY RUN COOLER AND FLATTER, which is close to a tautology once stated. The ISA-relevant question needs constant TOTAL POWER, or a real per-ISA activity mix, and neither is in this sweep.
the_obvious_next_experiment: Repeat at constant DIE POWER rather than constant density. That isolates the compaction effect the prediction was actually about, and it is the experiment the prediction should have specified. Cheap: 12 more points.
